Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading the question, naming it 'De obedientia' (on obedience).

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e113.summary: States the first of three parts into which the question on obedience is divided: whether obedience is a principal virtue distinct from the others.
claims: Obedience will first be examined as to whether it is a virtue in itself, distinct from other virtues.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e131.summary: States the second part of the division: whether the faithful are bound to obey even unbelieving lords.
claims: The question of obedience toward infidel lords will be treated second.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e141.summary: States the third part of the division: whether professed religious are bound to obey their prelates in all things.
claims: The question of a professed religious's obedience to his prelate will be treated third.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e157.summary: Rubric for Article 1, restating the question (whether obedience is a virtue) and announcing the affirmative conclusion in advance.
claims: Obedience is a virtue.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e166.summary: Bibliographic apparatus citing parallel loci in Aquinas (ST II-II q.104 a.2; Sent. II d.44 a.4) for the article's topic.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e171.summary: First objection (quia-argument) against obedience being a virtue: every virtue stands as a mean between two vices, but obedience occupies an extreme, since one can obey beyond what is owed without sinning, and even earn praise for it.
claims: Obedience appears to be an extreme, not a mean, since exceeding what is strictly owed in obedience does not incur vice and can be praiseworthy.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e194.summary: Second objection: even granting obedience is a virtue, it does not seem a determinate, special virtue, since 'to obey' just means 'to fulfill a precept,' and the acts of every virtue can fall under precept.
claims: If obedience is simply fulfilling any precept, and every virtuous act can be commanded, obedience cannot be a distinct special virtue.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e214.summary: Third objection: if obedience were a special virtue it would have to be one of the cardinal virtues or annexed to one, but no cardinal or annexed virtue goes by that name.
claims: Obedience is not named among the cardinal virtues or their annexes, so it cannot be a special virtue.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e225.summary: Fourth objection: the object of obedience seems to be a debt owed; but no virtue diminishes its own object, whereas to obey is precisely to remove or diminish a debt (by discharging it).
claims: Obeying appears to diminish the debt that is obedience's proper object, which would be improper for a virtue.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e236.summary: Fifth objection: obedience is identified with fulfilling mandates, and mandates are contained in law, so obedience would be identical with legal justice; but legal justice is a general virtue, so obedience (by this reasoning) should likewise be merely general, not special.
claims: Obedience collapses into legal justice and thus into a merely general virtue, on the assumption that mandates are simply the content of law.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e247.summary: Sed contra: obedience is called not merely a virtue but the 'mother' and 'preserver' of all the virtues, implying a special dignity beyond an ordinary virtue.
claims: Obedience is the mother and preserver of the virtues.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e256.summary: States the resolutio (the determined conclusion to be defended): obedience is not only a virtue but the mother and preserver of all virtues.
claims: Obedience is a virtue, and indeed the mother and preserver of all the virtues.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e266.summary: Announces the tripartite structure of the determinatio: (1) obedience is a special virtue because it is a part of justice; (2) materially considered, obedience can perform the acts of every virtue and even more than every virtue; (3) formally, despite being materially every virtue, obedience remains a special virtue distinct from the others.
claims: Obedience is formally a special virtue and a part of justice, while materially it can produce the acts of all the virtues and beyond.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e292.summary: Develops point (1): defines obedience as the relation of inferior to superior, or of servant to lord, noting that 'superiority' is broader than 'lordship' properly speaking, since a prelate should regard himself as ruling by virtue and charity in service rather than by domination.
claims: Obedience is essentially the relation of an inferior to a superior.
Not every superiority is properly dominion; a good prelate rules by virtue and charity, understanding himself as a servant.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e312.summary: Continues point (1): subjects and servants owe their superiors honor, fidelity, and (chiefly) the fulfilling of their mandates; this last is identified as constituting obedience itself, supported by Augustine's Rule and 1 Timothy 6 (already encoded as a quotation).
claims: Among the several things subjects owe their superiors (honor, fidelity, fulfillment of mandates), fulfilling mandates is what specifically constitutes obedience.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e354.summary: Concludes point (1): since justice is rendering another what is due, and fulfilling superiors' mandates is the chief thing subjects owe, obedience -- as the rendering of this debt -- is established as a part of justice.
claims: Obedience is a part of justice because it renders to a superior the debt of obeying his mandates.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e380.summary: Transitions to point (2) and develops it at length via an analogy with the sciences: just as one and the same subject-matter (e.g., matter) can fall under different sciences (physics, metaphysics) considered under different formal aspects, so one and the same virtuous act can belong to different virtues under different formal rationales; applies this to Aristotle's account of magnanimity (Ethics IV), which can perform the acts of every other virtue in a more excellent, honor-seeking way, distinguishing agents who act from delight in the act itself (the proper virtue) from the magnanimous agent who acts for the sake of honor.
claims: A single subject-matter can belong to several sciences or virtues under different formal rationales.
Magnanimity can materially perform the acts of every virtue, doing so in a more excellent manner because it acts for the sake of honor.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e513.summary: Applies the magnanimity analogy explicitly to obedience: just as magnanimity can perform every virtue's acts under the aspect of honor, obedience can perform every virtue's acts under the aspect of willing to fulfill a superior's command; illustrated by a soldier defending a fortress out of love of battle (fortitude) versus out of the will to obey a command (obedience), and by a religious who fasts from vow versus from personal inclination.
claims: Obedience, like magnanimity, can materially perform the acts of every virtue, but under its own proper formal rationale: the will to fulfill a superior's mandate.
The same external act can belong to different virtues depending on the agent's motivating formal rationale.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e590.summary: Argues that obedience is materially even more general than legal justice, since a superior can command the acts of every virtue and things beyond ordinary virtue (things good or bad merely because commanded or forbidden); distinguishes legal justice, which concerns written or promulgated law, from obedience, which extends to any manifested will of a superior, however communicated, citing 'the servant who knows his lord's will.'
claims: Obedience is materially a more general virtue than legal justice, because it extends to any manifestation of a superior's will, not only to promulgated law.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e658.summary: Develops point (3): parallels the science analogy again to show that, just as magnanimity is materially general but formally special (because it acts under the special rationale of honor), obedience is materially a general virtue but formally a special one, since it performs every virtuous act under the specific formal rationale of willing to fulfill a superior's mandate.
claims: Obedience is materially a general virtue but formally a special virtue, distinguished from all other virtues by its proper formal rationale (fulfilling a superior's mandate).

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e719.summary: Reply to objection 1: though virtue lies in a mean, it always leans toward the extreme less opposed to it; obedience is properly a mean, not an extreme, once one excludes obedience owed to God (which is unconditional) and recognizes that obedience to mere human prelates has limits (not owed against God or natural law); where in doubt, a subject should lean toward obeying rather than not, provided it can be done without sin.
claims: Obedience is a mean, not an extreme, once the unconditional case of obedience to God is set aside.
In doubtful cases a subject should incline toward obeying rather than refusing, if this can be done without sin.
concepts: obedience owed to God vs to men
benefit of the doubt in obedience

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e767.summary: Reply to objection 2: the objection only proves that obedience is a materially general virtue, not that it is formally general, nor that it can perform every virtuous act unconditionally -- only that it does so under the special rationale of willing to fulfill a command.
claims: Obedience's material generality does not entail formal generality; its acts are always performed under the special rationale of fulfilling a command.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e789.summary: Reply to objection 3: obedience is reduced to the cardinal virtue of justice as one of its parts; it is not itself a distinctly-named cardinal or annexed virtue because what it renders to a lord -- fulfillment of his mandate -- is precisely an act of justice.
claims: Obedience is a part of the cardinal virtue justice, not a separately-named cardinal or annexed virtue.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e815.summary: Reply to objection 4: the object of obedience is the superior's command itself; the obedient subject does not diminish the command but fulfills and perfects it, bringing it from potential ('in fieri') to actual ('in facto esse') existence, which is what the lord's will intends.
claims: Obeying perfects and actualizes the superior's command rather than diminishing it.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e840.summary: Reply to objection 5: obedience is indeed more general than legal justice, but only materially, not formally; formally both are special virtues, each acting under its own proper rationale -- legal justice to fulfill written law, obedience to fulfill whatever a superior commands, written or not.
claims: Obedience surpasses legal justice in material generality but not in formal generality; each remains a formally special virtue.

Gi9qrR-m203599-Dd1e150.summary: Establishes that obedience is a special virtue and a part of justice: it is defined as the relation of inferior to superior discharged through fulfilling the superior's mandate (making it a species of justice); materially it can perform -- and even exceed -- the acts of every other virtue (argued by analogy to the sciences and to Aristotelian magnanimity), yet formally it remains a distinct, special virtue because all such acts are performed under its own proper rationale, the will to fulfill a command. The five opening objections (drawn from the doctrine of virtue as a mean, the classification of cardinal/annexed virtues, the object of a virtue, and the relation to legal justice) are each resolved by this materialiter/formaliter distinction.
claims: Obedience is a special virtue, formally a part of justice.
Materially, obedience can perform the acts of every virtue and even acts beyond ordinary virtue, since a superior can command such things.
Formally, obedience remains distinct from all other virtues because it always acts under the specific rationale of fulfilling a superior's mandate.
Obedience is, in this material sense, a more general virtue than legal justice.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e870.summary: Rubric for Article 2, restating the question (whether the faithful are bound to obey unbelieving lords) and announcing the affirmative conclusion in advance.
claims: The faithful are bound to obey unbelieving lords.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e881.summary: Bibliographic apparatus citing parallel loci in Aquinas, Bonaventure, Richard of Mediavilla, and Durandus for the article's topic.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e892.summary: States the question and gives the first objection: it seems the faithful are not bound to obey unbelieving lords, since John 8 says 'if the Son has set you free, you will truly be free,' and all the baptized have put on Christ and been freed by him.
claims: Baptismal freedom in Christ seems to exempt believers from the obligation of obedience to any lord, especially an unbelieving one.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e922.summary: Second objection: Matthew 17 says sons are free from tribute; by baptism all become sons of God (the King of kings), and are therefore free from tribute and not bound to obey lords who demand it.
claims: Baptismal sonship of God implies exemption from tribute and obedience owed to human lords.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e944.summary: Third objection: since servitude was introduced on account of sin, and baptism and penance cleanse from sin, the cleansed are no longer servants and are not bound to obey anyone.
claims: Cleansing from sin through baptism or penance should remove the servitude that sin originally caused.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e957.summary: Fourth objection: what releases from a greater bond releases a fortiori from a lesser; the new law releases from the bond of the old law, so it should much more release from the bond of any mere human lord.
claims: Freedom from the old law's bond implies, a fortiori, freedom from subjection to any purely human lord.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e977.summary: Fifth objection: what was illicitly taken can licitly be reclaimed if possible; since many lords acquired dominion by usurpation and violence, such lords need not be obeyed if it is possible to resist.
claims: Dominion acquired unjustly by usurpation need not be obeyed, and may licitly be resisted or reclaimed.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e990.summary: Sed contra: 1 Peter 2 commands servants to be subject to their masters in all fear, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh (quotation already encoded).
claims: Scripture commands obedience even to harsh masters.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1001.summary: Further sed contra: 1 Timothy 6 commands those under the yoke of servitude to regard their masters as worthy of all honor (quotation already encoded); the gloss extends this explicitly to the yoke of unbelieving masters.
claims: Scripture, as glossed, extends the duty of honoring one's master even to unbelieving masters.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1013.summary: States the resolutio: one need not obey a prince who commands unjustly, but one must obey a prince -- whether a believer or unbeliever -- who commands justly.
claims: Obedience is not owed to an unjust command, but is owed to a just command regardless of the ruler's faith.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1024.summary: Announces the tripartite structure of the determinatio for this article: first, servitude itself (its kinds and origin); second, dominion (in what and how servants must obey it); third, faith (whether it removes or diminishes the justice owed to lords).

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1055.summary: Develops part 1: distinguishes natural servitude/dominion (per Aristotle's De Anima and Politics I, those strong in intellect but weak in body are naturally fit to rule, those strong in body but weak in intellect are naturally fit to serve, and it is mutually advantageous) from positive/actual servitude and dominion, which concerns actual legal-social status regardless of one's natural aptitude -- since many naturally fit to serve are in fact lords, and vice versa.
claims: There is a natural aptitude for ruling or serving, based respectively on strength of intellect or of body, which is mutually advantageous to both parties.
Actual (positive) servitude and dominion do not necessarily track natural aptitude for ruling or serving.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1140.summary: Continues part 1: on positive servitude's historical origin, citing Augustine (City of God 19) that the Latin word 'servus' derives from 'servare,' since captives spared in a just war ('by right of war') from execution became servants; but Giles notes this factual/etymological origin is not automatically a title of justice, and that true, just servitude arises instead from just inheritance, just purchase, or another just title.
claims: The word 'servus' derives from captives spared ('preserved') under the right of war.
Just servitude in reality (not merely by name) requires a just title such as inheritance, purchase, or another just cause, not mere conquest.
concepts: Augustine on the origin of servitude

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1201.summary: Develops part 2 on dominion: since all dominion as an order is from God, but its acquisition or exercise can be unjust, servants owe obedience only to those who are truly and justly lords using their power justly; discusses how an originally unjust dominion (as with Rome, per Augustine, City of God 19) can become just over time through the voluntary approval and use of the subjects, who come to benefit from and consent to the rule.
claims: All dominion as an order is from God, but unjust acquisition or use of power is not.
An originally unjust dominion can become just through the subjects' voluntary approval and beneficial use of it over time.
concepts: unjust vs just acquisition and use

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1310.summary: Concludes the discussion of unjust and rectified dominion: a subject is not bound to obey a prince who is unjust, but once an originally unjust dominion has become just through the subjects' approval, they may not thereafter withdraw from it without a just and legitimate cause.
claims: Subjects owe no obedience to an unjust ruler.
Once dominion has become just through subjects' approval, they cannot lawfully withdraw allegiance without a just cause.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1327.summary: Further distinguishes ways a justly-acquired dominion can become unjust in use: by commanding illicit things (which must never be obeyed, even at the cost of martyrdom, as martyrs refused imperial commands) or by imposing unusual burdens such as new taxes -- the latter noted as a matter more for jurists than theologians.
claims: A justly acquired dominion becomes unjust in use if it commands illicit acts, which must be refused even unto death.
Imposing novel, unusual burdens (e.g. new taxes) is a related but more juridical than theological question.
concepts: martyrdom and resistance to illicit commands

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1356.summary: Develops part 3 on faith: argues that Christ's grace and baptism liberate only spiritually (in the soul), not corporeally, since the baptized still die like the unbaptized; bodily liberation is deferred until the resurrection; supports this with Ezekiel 18 and Romans 3:22 (quotations already encoded), concluding that faith causes justice in believers and therefore increases, rather than removes, their obligation to render what is justly owed -- including obedience to lords, even unbelieving ones, per Christ's 'render unto Caesar.'
claims: Christian faith and baptism liberate the soul spiritually but not the body, which remains under temporal subjection until the resurrection.
Because faith causes justice in the believer, it increases rather than removes the obligation to render what is justly owed to a lord.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1445.summary: Reply to objection 1: through Christ and faith believers are spiritually freed and made sons of God, but this does not entail corporeal liberation from the yoke of their actual lords.
claims: Spiritual sonship and freedom in Christ do not entail freedom from bodily/civil subjection to a lord.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1458.summary: Reply to objection 2: what is ordained to subjects' utility does not remove their liberty; even gentile power served subjects' utility before the conversion of the nations, since human society requires some to govern others; now that many nations have entered the Church it would be reprehensible for a believer to seek to leave a faithful lord's rule for an unbeliever's; notes further that the Matthean text concerns tribute specifically, from which Christ and the apostles (holding all things in common, owning nothing proper) were exempt.
claims: Power ordained to subjects' benefit does not thereby remove their liberty.
The Matthean exemption from tribute applied specifically to Christ and the apostles' communal poverty, not as a general exemption for believers.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1493.summary: Reply to objection 3: original sin causes both a stain on the soul and bodily penalties; baptism and penance free from the stain of soul but not from bodily penalties; ecclesiastical dominion is ordered principally to spiritual good (with temporal effects only by redundancy), while secular dominion is ordered to temporal goods, so baptism and grace free believers from neither secular nor (still less) ecclesiastical dominion.
claims: Baptism removes the soul's stain from original sin but not its bodily penalties, among which is subjection to temporal (and ecclesiastical) dominion.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1526.summary: Reply to objection 4: one bond is dissolved by another only when the two are incompatible; the new law replaced the ceremonial and figural aspects of the old law because truth is incompatible with shadow, but the spiritual bond of baptismal servitude is fully compatible with the bodily bond of civil servitude to a lay lord, so the former does not dissolve the latter.
claims: The spiritual bond contracted in baptism is compatible with, and so does not dissolve, bodily civil servitude to a lay lord.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1556.summary: Reply to objection 5: one may licitly withdraw from an unjust dominion while it remains unjust, but once it has become just (as explained above), one may not withdraw except for a reasonable cause.
claims: Withdrawal from dominion is licit only while that dominion remains unjust; once legitimated, only a reasonable cause justifies withdrawal.

Gi9qrR-m203599-Dd1e863.summary: Determines that the faithful are bound to obey lords -- even unbelieving ones -- provided the lord's rule is just, resolving the question through a threefold analysis of servitude (distinguishing natural aptitude from positive/legal status, and tracing positive servitude's origin in the right of war while insisting true justice requires a proper title), dominion (distinguishing just from unjust acquisition and use, and showing how an originally unjust dominion can be legitimated by subjects' consent over time), and faith (arguing Christian liberty is spiritual only, leaving temporal subjection intact and indeed reinforcing the duty of justice). All five opening objections, which infer exemption from obedience from baptismal freedom, sonship of God, cleansing from sin, release from the old law, or unjust original acquisition, are answered by these distinctions.
claims: Obedience is owed to a lord's just command regardless of the lord's faith.
An unjust dominion need not be obeyed, but can become just, and thus binding, through the subjects' voluntary and beneficial acceptance of it over time.
Christian faith and baptism free the soul spiritually but do not remove the temporal/bodily obligations of justice and civil subjection.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1577.summary: Rubric for Article 3, restating the question (whether professed religious are bound to obey their prelates in all things) and announcing the affirmative conclusion in advance.
claims: Professed religious are bound to obey their prelates.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1593.summary: Bibliographic apparatus citing parallel loci in Aquinas, Bonaventure, Richard of Mediavilla, and Durandus for the article's topic.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1602.summary: States the question and gives the first objection: it seems religious must obey their prelates in everything, since Colossians 3 commands children to obey their parents in everything, and one owes even greater obedience to a spiritual father than to a carnal one.
claims: Scriptural command to obey parents 'in everything' seems to imply unconditional obedience to a spiritual superior a fortiori.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1625.summary: Second objection: St. Benedict holds that even if a prelate commands something impossible, the subject should still attempt to fulfill it, implying unconditional obedience.
claims: Benedict's rule implies subjects must attempt even impossible commands, suggesting unlimited obedience.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1634.summary: Third objection: every religious order has three essential vows (chastity, poverty, obedience); since chastity and poverty are vowed absolutely and without qualification, obedience must likewise be vowed absolutely, entailing obedience to the prelate in all things.
claims: The parallel structure of the three religious vows implies obedience, like chastity and poverty, is vowed without qualification.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1652.summary: Fourth objection: an inferior should not judge a superior, so it is not the subject's place to discern in which matters he must obey; it follows he must obey in everything.
claims: Since a subject may not judge his superior, he cannot licitly discriminate among commands, and so must obey unconditionally.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1665.summary: Fifth objection: every Christian is already bound to obey his spiritual prelates in some matters; if professed religious were bound to obey their prelates only in some matters (like ordinary Christians), religious life itself would be superfluous.
claims: If religious obedience were no more extensive than ordinary Christian obedience, the religious state would add nothing and be pointless.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1678.summary: Sed contra: Augustine's Rule states that the prelate should be honored before the community, but before God he lies prostrate at the subjects' feet -- implying limits on obedience when a prelate's command conflicts with God.
claims: A prelate's authority is itself subordinate to God, implying obedience has limits when a command opposes God.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1691.summary: Further sed contra: Acts 4 records Peter and John's answer to the Jewish authorities -- 'judge whether it is right in God's sight to obey you rather than God' (quotation already encoded) -- establishing that God must be obeyed above any human command.
claims: Obedience to God takes precedence over any human command.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1705.summary: States the resolutio: one must not obey a command against divine or natural law; one should not resist commands proper to one's state that pertain to positive law; in matters regular to religious observance and custom, religious owe obedience to their prelates by the law itself; in other matters obedience is not strictly owed but only counseled.
claims: Commands against divine or natural law are never to be obeyed.
Obedience is strictly owed, by the very law of religious life, only in regular and customary matters; elsewhere it is a matter of counsel, not precept.
concepts: obedience of precept vs of counsel

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1727.summary: Announces the tripartite framework for the determinatio: obedience will be considered (1) in comparison to the kinds of law (iura) on which it rests, (2) in comparison to the office of the one presiding to whom it is owed, and (3) in comparison to itself, i.e. its own internal modes.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1760.summary: Develops point (1a): distinguishes divine, natural, and positive law; identifies divine-law precepts (the first tablet -- worshipping only God, not swearing falsely, keeping the sabbath) as binding absolutely, such that not even God himself could dispense from them, since he could not permit the honor due him to be given to a creature, allow perjury, or release any creature from the subjection owed to him.
claims: Divine-law precepts of the first tablet bind absolutely; even God cannot dispense from them, since they concern what is owed to God essentially.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1810.summary: Develops points (1b) and (1c): natural-law precepts (the second tablet -- against killing, theft, adultery) can be dispensed only by God, not by any mere human, even the Pope (illustrated by Abraham/Isaac, the Israelites' spoiling of the Egyptians, and Hosea) -- so a religious must never obey a prelate commanding against divine or natural law; regarding positive law, since the same authority that establishes a law can also revoke or suspend it, subjects must obey a prelate who suspends his own regulation in a given case. Concludes the analysis of obedience's relation to the laws on which it rests.
claims: Only God, not any human authority including the Pope, can dispense from natural-law precepts.
A prelate who validly suspends his own positive regulation in a given case must be obeyed, since the authority to legislate includes the authority to revoke.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1908.summary: Develops point (2): obedience is owed to a superior only insofar as he presides in a given domain, not otherwise, illustrated by a military commander (obeyed in matters of war) and a paterfamilias (obeyed in household affairs); accordingly a religious prelate is owed obedience by his subjects in regular matters, including customs habitual to that particular religious order.
claims: Obedience is owed to a superior strictly within the domain of his office, not universally.
A religious superior is owed obedience specifically in regular and customary matters of that order.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1937.summary: Introduces point (3): announces that obedience, considered in relation to itself, can be taken in three ways -- as enjoined under precept, as counseled, and as prohibited.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e1951.summary: Elaborates the first two of the three modes: obedience 'under precept' extends to all regular observances and customary practices of the order (explaining the rationale of the year of probation, which lets both postulant and community discern fitness), and is called 'sufficient' obedience by the masters; obedience 'under counsel' extends further to anything licit and honest, even things that seem impossible, and is called 'perfect' obedience.
claims: Obedience of precept, called 'sufficient,' binds only to regular and customary observances.
Obedience of counsel, called 'perfect,' extends beyond precept to anything licit and honest, even apparently impossible things.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2006.summary: Elaborates the third mode: obedience is 'prohibited' or 'indiscreet' when a subject obeys a superior in illicit matters that cannot be done without sin (e.g. something against the rule or against God), and in such cases obedience must never be given; concludes that this threefold analysis resolves the article's proposed question.
claims: Obedience must never be given to a command that is illicit or sinful, regardless of the superior's status.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2026.summary: Rubric introducing an inserted 'lateral doubt' (dubitatio lateralis): whether one must always obey a higher prelate more than a lower one, with the conclusion stated in advance as affirmative.
claims: One must always obey a higher prelate more than a lower one (as a general rule, to be qualified).

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2046.summary: Bibliographic apparatus for the lateral dubitatio, citing Durandus, Raymond's Summa on obedience, and canon-law loci (Decretals).

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2055.summary: States the lateral question in full and gives an objection: citing a legal maxim concerning obedience to an orator/curator versus a proconsul versus an emperor, implying one must always obey the greater authority over the lesser.
claims: Legal precedent concerning nested civil authorities suggests one should always obey the higher power over the lower.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2081.summary: Sed contra objections: an Archbishop outranks a Bishop, yet in many matters the Bishop, not the Archbishop, is obeyed; likewise a Bishop outranks an Abbot, yet monks are bound to obey the Abbot more than the Bishop in many matters.
claims: Concrete ecclesiastical practice shows lower prelates are sometimes obeyed in preference to higher ones.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2098.summary: Further sed contra: spiritual power outranks lay power, yet if a layman commands payment of debts owed to him and a spiritual prelate commands the contrary, the subject should obey the lay lord.
claims: In matters proper to temporal debts, obedience is owed to the lay lord even against a contrary spiritual command.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2111.summary: States the resolutio for the lateral dubitatio: although absolutely speaking a higher prelate is always to be obeyed more than a lower one, by common law or by special privilege obedience is sometimes owed instead to a lower prelate in a given matter.
claims: The general rule of obeying the higher prelate admits exceptions grounded in common law or special privilege.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2127.summary: Develops the resolutio: draws on Pseudo-Dionysius (De Divinis Nominibus IV) -- in the universe there cannot be two things where one is not derived from the other, or both from a third -- and applies this to hierarchies of headship, distinguishing superiority 'in some respect' (where both derive from a common third) from superiority 'simply' (where one derives directly from the other); in the former case a subject need not always obey the higher; traces the ecclesiastical hierarchy (Pope, Patriarchs, Primates/Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots) to conciliar ordination ('what touches all must be approved by all'), with God alone as the absolute, simply-superior font to whom obedience is owed in all things.
claims: Hierarchical superiority can be either qualified (both parties deriving from a common source) or absolute (one deriving directly from the other), and only the latter always demands obedience.
The gradations of ecclesiastical prelacy (Pope, Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots) originate in conciliar ordination of the Church, not in a simple chain of derivation from one another.
God alone is the absolutely superior source to whom obedience is owed in everything.
concepts: quod omnes tangit ab omnibus approbari debet

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2229.summary: Replies to the lateral dubitatio's sed-contra objections concerning Archbishop/Bishop and Abbot: though a subject owes more obedience to the Pope than to an Archbishop or Bishop (and a monk more to the Pope than to his Abbot, admitting no exemption there), in other matters exemption can be granted by common law or special privilege, which explains why lower prelates are sometimes obeyed preferentially, without contradicting the general rule.
claims: Obedience to the Pope admits no exemption, but obedience to intermediate prelates can be modified by legitimate exemptions granted through common law or privilege.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2268.summary: Replies to the third lateral objection (spiritual vs. lay power): the two headships are not of the same kind (ratio), a point resolved by the Gospel command to 'render unto Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's' (quotation already encoded); notes that the principal question and the lateral dubitatio are now both resolved, leaving only the original article's objections to be answered.
claims: Spiritual and temporal power are not commensurable kinds of authority, so obedience to one does not straightforwardly override obedience to the other in its proper domain.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2290.summary: Reply to the article's first objection (Col 3, 'obey in everything'): clarifies that 'in everything' pertains only to matters within the father's proper headship, not absolutely and unconditionally; if a father commands something against God, one must not only refuse but resist; the same principle applies to religious and their prelates.
claims: Scriptural commands to obey 'in everything' are limited to the proper domain of the superior's authority, not absolute; a command against God must be resisted, not merely refused.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2317.summary: Replies to the second and third objections: (2) St. Benedict's rule concerns 'perfect' obedience under counsel (extending even to matters of food and other things possible without sin), yet a subject may still licitly protest a possible-but-non-obligatory command he is not bound to by precept; (3) unlike chastity and poverty, which have a determinate, specific subject-matter, obedience has a very broad subject-matter (since, absolutely speaking, a superior could command illicit or improper things), so a subject is not bound, or does not vow, to obey in absolutely everything.
claims: St. Benedict's teaching concerns obedience of counsel, not precept, and does not preclude licit protest of non-obligatory commands.
Obedience differs from chastity and poverty in having an indeterminately broad matter, which is why the vow of obedience cannot be simply universal.
concepts: determinate vs general matter of a vow

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2359.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: regarding matters prescribed by the rule, constitutions, or ordinary custom of the order, the subject has no right to judge; but if notably grave or unusual things were commanded (e.g. sleeping on bare ground), not customary to that religious order, the subject may licitly protest.
claims: A subject has no discretion regarding ordinary regular/constitutional matters, but may licitly object to notably unusual or excessively grave commands not customary to the order.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2377.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: all Christians, by renouncing Satan and professing the Christian life (citing Ephesians 4:24, already encoded), are already bound in some respects; but religious are more bound, since beyond this baptismal commitment they are obligated to the three essential vows of religion contained in their rule -- preserving the distinctiveness of the religious state.
claims: All Christians are bound by baptismal renunciation, but professed religious are additionally and more strictly bound by the three essential vows, which preserves the distinctive purpose of religious life.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2397.summary: Rubric introducing the first of a series of appended 'literal doubts' (dubitationes litterales), a distinct genre glossing specific words or arguments in Peter Lombard's text of the Sentences rather than continuing the article's disputational structure.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2402.summary: First literal dubitatio: raises and resolves an objection to the order of Lombard's text -- since the discussion of the act of sinning ('post praedicta') seems to precede treatment of the power to sin, though potency should logically precede act as cause precedes effect -- by distinguishing the order proper to things (ordo rerum, where cause precedes effect) from the order proper to teaching (ordo doctrinae, where effects, being better known to us, are sometimes treated first, as here, since powers are known through their acts).
claims: The order of exposition in a text can legitimately follow the order of teaching (effects before causes, as better known to us) rather than the order of being (causes before effects).

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2441.summary: Rubric introducing the second literal dubitatio.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2447.summary: Second literal dubitatio: questions why the text speaks of 'the power to sin' in the singular rather than the plural, since multiple faculties can concur materially in an act of sin; resolves that although several powers can concur materially in sinning, formally and principally it is the will alone by which one sins or acts well.
claims: Although several faculties can materially contribute to a sinful act, the will alone is the formal and principal power by which one sins or acts rightly.
concepts: will as formal cause of sin/merit
material vs formal concurrence of faculties

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2471.summary: Rubric introducing the third literal dubitatio.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2480.summary: Third literal dubitatio: raises an objection to the text's claim that 'a bad will is not from God in us,' since will and free choice denote one and the same power, and free choice is from God in us; resolves by distinguishing 'will' as sometimes denoting the potency (power), which is from God, and sometimes the act (the ordinary sense in speech, e.g. 'this is my will' = 'I will this'), so that the power to sin is from God while the actual sinful act, or will taken as act, is not.
claims: 'Will' is equivocal between the potency (which is from God) and the act (which, when sinful, is not from God); the objection trades on this ambiguity.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2515.summary: Rubric introducing the fourth literal dubitatio.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2520.summary: Fourth literal dubitatio: presses further on the prior solution, objecting that the very act of sinning, insofar as it is an act, is from God; resolves with a refined distinction -- the potency to sin is from God simply/absolutely and only 'not from God' in a qualified sense (secundum quid), whereas the defective sinful act is simply 'not from God' and only 'from God' in a qualified, material sense (insofar as it is merely an act), because potency formally denotes a real being while the sinful act formally denotes the defect itself.
claims: The potency to sin is simply from God (not from God only secundum quid); the defective act of sin is simply not from God (from God only secundum quid, materially, as an act).
concepts: potency as being, defect as privation

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2562.summary: Rubric introducing the fifth literal dubitatio.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2568.summary: States the fifth literal dubitatio's topic: a doubt concerning the text's phrase 'if by many testimonies of the saints.'

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2577.summary: Objection: the Master's (Lombard's) proof seems invalid, since the authorities he cites concern the power of prelacy, not the power to sin.
claims: The authorities Lombard cites appear to address a different topic (prelacy) than the one they are meant to prove (power to sin).

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2588.summary: Resolves the objection: every man is in some sense his own prelate as long as he is a wayfarer capable of good or evil, since God left man in the hand of his own counsel and set fire and water before him; indeed, headship over others derives its origin from headship over oneself, since one who cannot rule himself ought not rule another -- so the inference from the power to sin to the power of prelacy (and conversely) is not improper when rightly understood.
claims: Every person exercises a kind of self-governance ('prelacy over oneself') as a moral agent capable of choosing good or evil.
Authority over others is grounded in, and derives from, the capacity to govern oneself.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2625.summary: Rubric introducing the sixth literal dubitatio.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2630.summary: States the sixth literal dubitatio: a doubt on the text's citation 'through me kings reign... and tyrants' (Proverbs 8, already encoded), asking what distinguishes a king from a tyrant.
claims: A doubt is raised as to the difference between legitimate kingship and tyranny.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2641.summary: Resolves the sixth dubitatio by assigning three differences between king and tyrant: the king intends the public good, the tyrant a private good; the king intends the good of those he rules, the tyrant his own good; the king presides over his subjects as over sons, the tyrant as over slaves.
claims: A legitimate king intends the common good and treats subjects as sons; a tyrant intends private good and treats subjects as slaves.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2662.summary: Rubric introducing the seventh and final literal dubitatio.

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2667.summary: Seventh literal dubitatio and its resolution, concluding the entire work: objects that since the devil's power is also said to be from God (per the Apostle), one should not resist his power either; resolves that the Apostle (Rom. 13) speaks of the power of prelacy, which -- like obedience of counsel -- must not be resisted but obeyed unless it commands against God, whereas the devil possesses no true headship over anyone, only a usurped one to the extent one consents to him through sin, so resisting sin is precisely how one withdraws from the devil's power; the text then closes the commentary on Book II of the Sentences with a doxology to Christ.
claims: The Apostle's teaching on not resisting authority concerns the legitimate power of prelacy, not the devil's usurped and merely sin-dependent power.
The devil's power over a person exists only insofar as that person consents to him through sin, so resisting sin is what withdraws one from his power.
concepts: usurped power grounded in consent to sin

Gi9qrR-m203599-d1e2728.summary: Editorial/printer's colophon closing the printed edition: notes that the work lay unpublished/obscure for nearly a century after its single early printing (roughly forty years after the invention of printing), followed by 'Laus Deo.' A paratextual note external to Giles's argument, belonging to the print history of the text rather than to its doctrinal content.

Gi9qrR-m203599-Dd1e1570.summary: Determines the scope of a professed religious's duty to obey his prelate, arguing against unconditional obedience 'in everything' through a threefold comparison: to the kind of law obedience rests on (divine-law precepts bind absolutely and admit no dispensation even by God; natural-law precepts can be dispensed only by God, never a mere human including the Pope; positive regulations can be suspended by the authority that made them), to the office of the one presiding (obedience is owed only within a superior's proper domain, and for religious specifically in regular and customary matters), and to obedience's own three internal modes (of precept/'sufficient', of counsel/'perfect', and prohibited/'indiscreet', the last never to be followed). The five opening objections for unconditional obedience are each answered by these distinctions. The article's disputation is followed by an inserted lateral dubitatio on whether a higher prelate must always be obeyed over a lower one (resolved via a Dionysian principle distinguishing qualified from absolute hierarchical superiority, applied to the structure of ecclesiastical office), and then by seven literal dubitationes glossing specific words and arguments in Peter Lombard's text (on textual order, the unity of the will as sinning-power, the sense in which a bad will is or is not 'from God,' the difference between king and tyrant, and the distinction between the legitimate power of prelacy and the devil's merely usurped power) -- the last of which closes the entire commentary on Book II of the Sentences with a doxology, followed by the printer's colophon.
claims: Religious owe unconditional obedience to their prelates only within regular and customary matters governed by positive religious law; obedience is never owed against divine or natural law, and beyond regular matters it is a matter of counsel, not strict precept.
Hierarchical obedience admits exceptions to the rule of always obeying the higher prelate, grounded in common law or special privilege, except with respect to the Pope and (ultimately) God.
A distinction between the power/potency to sin (from God) and the actual sinful act (not from God) resolves several textual difficulties in the Lombard's discussion of the origin of evil willing.
Legitimate prelatial power must be obeyed (unless commanding against God), while the devil's power is merely usurped through the sinner's own consent and is properly resisted.

Gi9qrR-m203599.summary: Synthesizes the whole of Question 2, 'De obedientia' (Book II, distinction 44, question 2), across its three articles and its appended dubitationes: obedience is first established as a special virtue and a part of justice, materially embracing but formally distinct from every other virtue (Art. 1); it is then shown to bind the faithful even toward unbelieving lords, provided the lord's rule is just, since Christian liberty is spiritual rather than temporal (Art. 2); finally, the extent of a professed religious's obedience to his prelate is delimited by the kind of law involved, the superior's proper domain, and obedience's own modes of precept, counsel, and prohibition, with an inserted dubitatio on hierarchical obedience and a closing series of literal glosses on the Lombard's text that bring the commentary on Book II to its conclusion.
claims: Obedience is a special virtue, formally a part of justice, that can materially perform the acts of every other virtue.
The faithful owe obedience to any lord, believer or unbeliever, whose command is just; unjust dominion need not be obeyed but can become binding through the subjects' consent over time.

Professed religious owe strict obedience to their prelates only within the regular and customary matters of their order and never against divine or natural law; beyond this, obedience is a matter of counsel rather than precept.
